header.title: Contra caducum morbum (P) (Paris, Bibl. Nationale, Ms. nouv. acq. lat. 229): AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Anonymous
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's urn:rem:anonymous:m048p:norm, from the Referenzkorpus Mittelhochdeutsch, ReM 2.1 (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. notes.9v.23: donerdiutige, dietêwige and pontum patum are kept as words of power; the first two may be German epithets (something like 'thunder-…' and 'eternal for the people'), but their sense is uncertain. 9v.29 alsô tuon ich dich: literally 'so do I you', with 'drive' understood.

nodes.text: Against the falling sickness. Go to the sick person as he lies, and from the left
as far as the right side, pacing; and so, standing over him, say three times: *donerdiutige*,
*dietêwige*. Then the devil's son came onto Adam's bridge and
split a stone into firewood. Then Adam's son came and struck
the devil's son against a bush. Peter sent Paul, his
brother, to bind vein to vein, *pontum patum*. He drove out
Satan. So I [drive] you, unclean spirit, from this
Christian body. As quickly may relief come to this Christian
body as I touch the earth with my hands. And
touch the earth with both hands, and say the Our Father. After this, leap across to the right,
and with your right foot touch his right side and say: “Stand up! What was the matter
with you? God commanded this of you.” Do this three times, and soon you will see the sick person
